unit.title: Parts of the soul II
unit.needIt: Understanding how your brain works helps you see why you make quick mistakes or feel sudden urges. It helps you catch your own habits before they lead to bad choices.
unit.why: Our brains have two systems. One is fast and automatic, like a reflex. The other is slow and logical, like solving a math problem. Sometimes, our old habits act like a 'ghost' that pulls us toward a choice even when we know better.
unit.outcome: Identify when your automatic habits are overriding your logical goals.
unit.reachesYou: You feel this when you grab a snack even though you are on a diet. You see it when you reach for your phone out of habit before you even think about it.
unit.do: Notice one time today when you do something automatically without thinking. Stop for a second and ask yourself why you did it.

quiz.q: How did Thorndike's subjects react to complex characters?
quiz.why: The lecture states that complex characters caused a massive drop in performance.
quiz.quote: Presenting people with problems that were formally identical, but which differed in terms of the complexity of the characters used to represent them, produced a massive decrement in performance.

quiz.why: An alief is a habitual way of responding to the world that can override current beliefs.

partials: System One is fast and automatic.
System Two is slow and effortful.
Framing changes how we see choices.
Habits can override our current beliefs.
Aliefs are habitual ways of responding.
crystal.key: Our brains use automatic habits (aliefs) that can override our conscious logic.

decoys.why: The lecture shows that System One can be biased by framing and habits.

decoys.text: Aliefs are the same as logical beliefs.

crystal.aha: The automatic 'alief' system often acts faster than our conscious 'System Two' logic.
